slots.title: September payrolls add 29K vs 90K expected
slots.body:
US employers added 29,000 jobs in September.

Economists had expected about 90,000; August was revised context at 133,000.

The unemployment rate — the share of people in the labor force without work — came in at 4.2%, above the 4.1% forecast and up from 4.1% in August.

Private payrolls rose 46,000 vs an 85,000 estimate.

After the 12:30 p.m.
ET release, the session closed with:
- $SPY proxy ^GSPC +0.7% to 7,723.49
- Nasdaq ^IXIC +1.2% to 27,190.86
- VIX -6.6% to 15.31

Coverage tied the move to softer hiring and slower wage prints vs expectations.

What part of the report do you watch first — headline payrolls or the unemployment rate?

slots.title: Trump rules out US diesel export ban
slots.body:
Trump said Friday he is not going to authorize an export ban on diesel.

That came hours after G7 members agreed to release diesel and crude from emergency reserves.

Oil-linked moves on the session included:
- Brent crude -0.1% to 102.25
- USO -1.8% to 147.37

The prior day’s coverage had focused on whether Washington might restrict diesel exports amid supply talk.

Does energy policy belong in your macro checklist, or do you treat it separately from jobs and rates?

slots.title: Hourly pay up 0.1% MoM, 3.0% YoY
slots.body:
Average hourly earnings — what workers are paid per hour on average — rose 0.1% from August to September.

The consensus had been 0.3% month over month; August was 0.3%.

Year over year, pay was up 3.0% vs a 3.2% estimate and 3.1% prior.

Government payrolls fell by 17,000 jobs; the estimate had been +15,000, with +44,000 in the prior month.

The broader underemployment rate (U-6), which includes discouraged workers and part-timers who want full-time work, was 7.6% vs a 7.7% forecast.

September’s full labor print dropped at 12:30 p.m.
ET on 2026-10-02.

Which wage line matters more for you — the monthly bump or the year-over-year trend?

slots.title: U.S. session recap — Oct. 2, 2026
slots.body:
The September U.S. jobs report landed at 12:30 p.m.
ET with nonfarm payrolls at 29,000 — well below the 90,000 estimate — and the unemployment rate at 4.2% versus 4.1% previously.
Average hourly earnings rose 0.1% month over month and 3.0% year over year.
Market coverage described stocks finishing higher as that combination reduced urgency around another near-term Federal Reserve rate increase.

The S&P 500 rose 0.7%, closing at 7,723.49 after a range between 7,700.51 and 7,754.67.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 0.5% to 51,176.96.
The Russell 2000 gained 0.9% to 2,832.90.

The Nasdaq Composite led the large indexes with a 1.2% gain to 27,190.86; the session high at 27,353.68 matched the index’s year high in the injected data.

The CBOE Volatility Index fell 6.6% to 15.31, from a prior close of 16.39, with an intraday low of 15.30.

Among megacaps, $TSLA rose 4.7% to $370.59 on heavy volume.
$ASML gained 3.3% to $1,867.31; $AMD and $TSM each rose 3.0%, to $633.91 and $472.78.
$ORCL closed up 3.1% at $142.30.
$GOOGL and $GOOG each rose about 1.6%, to $343.50 and $340.35.
$AMZN added 1.3% to $251.52.
$NVDA finished up 1.3% at $233.95.

Healthcare was the weakest Nasdaq sector average in the set, at -1.1%.
Utilities averaged -1.5%.
Financial Services averaged -0.6%.
Industrials averaged +2.9%, Consumer Cyclical +1.0%, and Basic Materials +1.2%.
Technology averaged -0.4% despite several large chip-related gainers.

$NKE was down 3.6% to $33.87 among active names.
$NFLX slipped 1.2% to $67.06.
$JNJ fell 1.0% to $256.03.

Overseas indexes in the snapshot were mixed: Japan’s Nikkei 225 was down 0.9%; the Hang Seng was down 2.6%.
The FTSE 100 rose 0.3%.
The Germany proxy in the data (EWG) rose 1.2%.

Gold futures fell 1.0% to $4,162.30.
The U.S. Oil Fund (USO) was down 1.8% at $147.37.
Brent crude was roughly flat, down 0.1% at $102.25.
The dollar proxy (UUP) slipped 0.2% to $28.89.
Bitcoin was up 0.2% at $84,637.40.

Treasury yield levels in the injected snapshot were dated 2026-09-30, with the 10-year at 5.3% and the 2s10s spread at 0.41 percentage points.
Same-day headline coverage noted Treasury yields climbing into the close.

Reuters reported that President Trump said he would not authorize a diesel export ban, hours after G7 countries agreed to release diesel and crude from emergency reserves — context that sat alongside weaker oil-linked proxies in the cross-asset block.

No earnings entries were listed in the injected earnings calendar for this bundle.
The economic calendar for the session also included U-6 unemployment at 7.6%, manufacturing payrolls +9,000, and government payrolls -17,000.

slots.title: Weekly jobless claims after September payrolls
slots.body:
The Sep/26 week’s initial jobless claims came in at 197K versus a 200K consensus and 198K prior, in a release dated Oct 1 at 12:30 ET.

Continuing claims for the Sep/19 week were 1701K versus a 1730K estimate and 1712K prior, in the same calendar block.

Friday’s September payrolls report (separate release) showed 29K jobs added versus a 90K estimate and 133K prior, with unemployment at 4.2% versus a 4.1% estimate.

That payroll print is fixed; the next labor filing to watch in the weekly series is the initial claims update after the 197K Sep/26 reading.

Which labor number do you track first after a payrolls week — claims or unemployment?

Hours later, the same Reuters item quotes President Trump saying he will not authorize a US diesel export ban.
